questions.q: Why does Terraform need a remote backend with locking before it can safely run from CI?
options: So two pipeline runs (or a pipeline run and someone's laptop) can't write to the state file at the same time and corrupt it
So the Terraform binary downloads faster
Because GitHub Actions requires all state to be stored in GitHub itself
Because Terraform cannot read YAML files without one
questions.explain: A remote backend like S3 with a DynamoDB lock table ensures only one Terraform run can write state at a time, preventing corruption from concurrent runs.

questions.q: What three checks does Northbridge Retail's pipeline run on every pull request that touches infrastructure code?
options: terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, and terraform plan
docker build, docker push, and kubectl apply
npm install, npm test, and npm build
terraform apply, terraform destroy, and terraform import
questions.explain: fmt, validate, and plan are all read-only checks that run on every PR — none of them change real infrastructure.

questions.q: Why is `terraform apply` run in a separate job from `plan`, gated behind a GitHub environment?
options: Because apply and plan cannot run on the same operating system
So a human must manually approve the one step that actually changes real infrastructure, after reading the plan
Because GitHub Actions limits jobs to one step each
To make the pipeline run faster
questions.explain: Plan is read-only and safe to run automatically; apply changes real infrastructure, so it's deliberately gated behind a required manual approval.

questions.q: How does the CI pipeline authenticate to AWS to run Terraform, according to this lesson?
options: It doesn't authenticate — AWS trusts any GitHub Actions run automatically
By emailing the credentials to the platform team before each run
Through OIDC federation, which issues a short-lived role at run time instead of using a stored long-lived access key
By storing the AWS root account password as a GitHub secret
questions.explain: The `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` action with `id-token: write` permission uses OIDC so AWS issues a short-lived credential — no long-lived access key is stored in the repo.

questions.q: Where does the `terraform plan` output go so a reviewer can see what would change before approving a pull request?
options: It's emailed to the entire engineering organization
It's deleted immediately after the job finishes
It's only visible by SSHing into the CI runner
It's posted as a comment on the pull request itself
questions.explain: Posting the plan as a PR comment lets a reviewer read exactly what Terraform would create, modify, or destroy before approving the change.
